intro: To create a numbered list in Google Docs on Mac, click where the list starts and then click the Numbered list button in the toolbar. The shortcut is ⌘ + Shift + 7, and if you don't see the button, click More first.
tldr: Click where the list starts, then click the Numbered list button, or press ⌘ + Shift + 7.
If the button is missing, click More in the toolbar first.
Press Tab to nest an item. Press Enter twice to go back to the main list.
To restart at 1, double-click the first number and use Format > Bullets & numbering > List options.
Lazur can point at the button or walk you through a step, but it does not click for you.

blocks.text: A numbered list in Google Docs takes one click or one shortcut. The harder part is what happens after the first item. Nested items and numbers that refuse to restart are where people usually get stuck. This page covers the basic steps first, then those spots, then how Lazur can point at things on your screen while you work.
Start a numbered list from the toolbar or the keyboard

The toolbar route is the one Google documents. Click on the line where the list should begin. Then click the Numbered list button. Google's help page for computers describes this exact sequence, so it is the safest place to start.

The keyboard route is faster once you know it. The shortcut is ⌘ + Shift + 7 on a Mac. Google's keyboard shortcuts page lists it under paragraph formatting, next to the bulleted list and checklist shortcuts. Windows and Chrome OS use Ctrl + Shift + 7 for the same job, so the only change for a Mac is the modifier key.

blocks.title: Check the cursor first
blocks.text: If the shortcut does nothing, click inside the document text first. The cursor has to be in the document before the shortcut can act. Then press ⌘ + Shift + 7 again.

blocks.text: Nested numbered list in Google Docs on Mac: Tab in, Enter twice out

Nesting turns a sub-point into its own level. Press Tab at the start of an item to indent it. Type the sub-items, then press Enter twice to return to the main list. A worked example makes this clearer.

Say you are writing a grant report with three sections. Section 1 has two sub-points and section 2 has one. Type the three main items first. Then move the cursor to the second line, press Tab, and type the sub-points. After the sub-points, press Enter twice and continue with section 3.

Check the numbers after every indent. If a nested list starts at the wrong number, use the restart steps in the next section. Do not retype the numbers by hand. Hand-typed numbers stop following the list the moment you add an item.

blocks.title: If Tab does not work for you
blocks.text: Google's list help names Tab and Enter twice. It does not mention Shift + Tab or the indent buttons for lists. The keyboard shortcuts page does list ⌘ + ] to increase indent and ⌘ + [ to decrease it, so try those if you need them.
Restart numbering in Google Docs on Mac, or continue an earlier list

Numbering trouble shows up most when you reuse a list. A quiz with five questions followed by an answer key is a common case. The answer key should start at 1 again, but Docs may carry on counting from the quiz. That is the moment to restart numbering.

Double-click the first number of the list to select that list. Then choose Format > Bullets & numbering > List options > Restart numbering. Type the start number in the box and click OK. The list counts from that number.

The reverse case is a list that should keep going. Say your steps are split into two lists by a paragraph of explanation. Pick List options > Continue previous numbering so the second list picks up the count from the first. You only need to find that menu once.
Switch between numbers, bullets and checklists

Google Docs lets you change the list type after you create the list. Select the list, then go to Format > Bullets & numbering and pick the style you want. For speed, use the shortcuts: ⌘ + Shift + 7 for numbers, ⌘ + Shift + 8 for bullets, and ⌘ + Shift + 9 for a checklist.

blocks.text: Mistakes people make with a numbered list on Mac

The most common mistake is typing the numbers yourself. A typed 1. and 2. is plain text. It will not renumber when you add an item above it. Use the toolbar button or ⌘ + Shift + 7 so Docs handles the count.
The second mistake is mixing up Tab and Enter. Tab nests an item. Enter starts the next item at the same level. Check which key you pressed before you assume the list is broken.
The third mistake is using a bulleted list when order matters. Numbers tell a reader that the sequence counts. Use bullets only for items with no order, such as a set of options or a list of tools.

blocks.title: Menu names on your screen
blocks.text: Google's help pages describe no Mac-only differences for these menus. If a name on your screen looks different, press Option + / and type the name you see. That opens the tool finder, which Google used to call Search the menus.
When the button or the shortcut is missing

A missing button usually means the toolbar is hiding it. Click More, as Google's help says. If you still cannot see it, use the shortcut, which works from the document text and does not need the toolbar.

Browser problems are harder to pin down. Google's system requirements page asks you to update your browser to one of the two most recent versions. For offline work Google requires Chrome or Microsoft Edge, so Chrome is a safe browser to test with.

Some sites suggest disabling extensions, clearing the cache or trying a private window. Google's documentation does not list those fixes. Try them only after you update the browser, and treat them as guesses rather than confirmed fixes.
Using Lazur for the parts you get stuck on

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac. It lives in the notch and listens and looks at your screen only while you hold the shortcut. Hold ⌥ ⌘ and ask your question out loud. Lazur answers out loud too.

Ask where something is and Lazur draws a circle and a label around it on your screen. For this page, ask where the Numbered list button is, and Lazur circles it. If the button is hidden, ask where More is, and Lazur points there.

Ask how instead, and Lazur guides you one click at a time. It waits for each click before it moves on. Say walk me through restarting numbering, and it takes you through Format, then Bullets & numbering, then List options. It does not click any of them for you.

Lazur explains things and points at them. It does not edit your document, and it is not a plugin or add-in for Google Docs. For voice dictation inside Docs, see [voice typing in Google Docs](/how-to/use-voice-typing-in-google-docs). To try Lazur, see the [download page](/download) and check [pricing](/pricing) before you decide.
Numbers or bullets: which list fits your page

Use numbers when order matters. Steps in a procedure, rankings and numbered citations all need the count. Use bullets when the items form a set with no order, such as a list of tools or a set of options.

Numbers also help during review. A reviewer can write item 4 is wrong in a comment, and both of you know which line that means. Bullets make that reference harder to use. Numbered footnotes work the same way, and the steps are in [how to insert a footnote in Google Docs](/how-to/insert-a-footnote-in-google-docs).
Once the list works, the next common task is usually a header or footer. Those steps are in [how to add a header and footer in Google Docs](/how-to/add-a-header-and-footer-in-google-docs).

faq.question: Where is the Numbered list button in Google Docs on Mac?
faq.answer: Google's help page for computers says to click More if the button is not visible. Look in More for Numbered list, or press ⌘ + Shift + 7 instead.

faq.question: Is the numbered list shortcut different on a Mac?
faq.answer: Yes. The Mac uses ⌘ where Windows and Chrome OS use Ctrl. The numbered list shortcut is ⌘ + Shift + 7 on a Mac and Ctrl + Shift + 7 on Windows and Chrome OS.

faq.question: Can I make a numbered list in Google Docs on Mac without a browser?
faq.answer: Google's pages describe Docs as a browser app and show no separate Mac app. For offline editing, Google requires Chrome or Microsoft Edge, the Google Docs Offline extension, and offline turned on in Drive settings.

faq.question: Why does my numbered list start at 4 instead of 1?
faq.answer: The list may be continuing an earlier list. Double-click the first number, then go to Format > Bullets & numbering > List options > Restart numbering, enter 1, and click OK.

faq.question: Does Google Docs on Mac need macOS Ventura?
faq.answer: Google's system requirements page lists macOS Ventura 13.0 or higher. That requirement is tied to Drive for desktop, which syncs Docs files, not to Docs open in a browser.

faq.question: Can Lazur make the numbered list for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur points at the Numbered list button, explains the menu path, or guides you one click at a time when you ask how. It does not click for you or edit your document.

faq.question: Does Lazur watch my screen all the time?
faq.answer: No. Lazur listens and looks only while you hold ⌥ ⌘. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer and are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models.

steps.name: Open the document in your browser
steps.text: Open the document in a browser on your Mac. Docs runs in the browser, and Google's official pages show no separate Mac app for it.

steps.name: Click where the list should start
steps.text: Click on the line where the first item belongs. If the line is empty, type the first item there. The list starts on that line.

steps.name: Click the Numbered list button
steps.text: Find the Numbered list button in the toolbar and click it. If you do not see it, click More and look there. The current line becomes item 1.

steps.name: Or use the keyboard shortcut
steps.text: Press ⌘ + Shift + 7 to start a numbered list on the current line. Windows and Chrome OS use Ctrl + Shift + 7 for the same action.

steps.name: Type your items and press Enter
steps.text: Type each item, then press Enter to start the next number. Keep going until the list is complete. Google Docs supplies each new number for you.

steps.name: Indent an item to nest it
steps.text: Place the cursor at the start of an item and press Tab. That item moves into a nested list. Type the sub-items, then check their numbers before you go on.

steps.name: Return to the main list
steps.text: Press Enter twice to leave the nested list and return to the main list. Google's help page documents this pattern for nested items.

steps.name: Change the list type if needed
steps.text: Select the list, then go to Format > Bullets & numbering and choose the list type you want. Use this to switch a numbered list to bullets.

steps.name: Restart numbering at a new number
steps.text: Double-click the first number in the list. Then open List options, choose Restart numbering, type the start number, and click OK.

steps.name: Continue an earlier list instead
steps.text: If the list should keep counting from a list above it, choose List options > Continue previous numbering. Use this when a paragraph of text split one list into two.

shortcuts.action: Tool finder, formerly Search the menus

troubleshooting.problem: The Numbered list button is not in the toolbar
troubleshooting.fix: Click More in the toolbar. Google's help page says the button may be hidden there. You can also press ⌘ + Shift + 7.

troubleshooting.problem: The second list keeps counting from the first
troubleshooting.fix: Double-click the first number of the second list, then use List options > Restart numbering and enter 1. Use Continue previous numbering only when you want the count to carry on.
Click inside the document text first, then press ⌘ + Shift + 7 again. If it still fails, use the Format menu and choose Bullets & numbering.

troubleshooting.problem: A menu name on screen differs from this page
troubleshooting.fix: Google's help pages describe no Mac-only menu differences. Press Option + / and type the name you see to find the matching command in the tool finder.

troubleshooting.problem: Docs will not respond or will not type properly
troubleshooting.fix: Google's official help lists no fix for this. Update your browser to a recent version, then test in Chrome. Advice to clear the cache or disable extensions comes from third-party sites and is not confirmed by Google.
